text: This is a real flame, burning aboard the International Space Station. No up. No down. Just a sphere of fire.
In microgravity, fire does not rise, and our Earth-based instincts about it no longer apply.
I'm Fahim Foysal, and for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, I took on the Flame in Freefall challenge.
This is FlameGuard A I. It turns NASA's own experiments from the space station into fire safety insight that anyone can use, with one promise: it never invents a number.
Why does it matter? A spacecraft is a sealed world. NASA's Flame Extinguishment Experiment asked a vital question: below what oxygen level will a flame refuse to keep burning?
Its test atmospheres matched the station's normal cabin, the air used before spacewalks, and the richest oxygen level proposed for future exploration vehicles.
Between 2009 and 2011, NASA burned two hundred and seventy four fuel droplets in orbit. One hundred and eighty six flames went out on their own. Eighty eight kept burning.
But those answers are buried in a three hundred page report and raw data tables. No one can simply ask: under these conditions, will this fire survive? So I built a tool that can.
Pick a fuel, the oxygen, a suppressant and the droplet size. A machine learning model, trained and tested on NASA's data, estimates the chance the flame keeps burning.
Then it explains itself: what pushed the risk up or down, how close you are to real tests, and how often it was right before.
On tests it never saw, it ranks a burning flame above an extinguished one ninety two percent of the time. When it calls high risk, eighty seven percent of those flames really kept burning.
The What If Lab puts two scenarios head to head, with real NASA tests overlaid as a reality check.
Every NASA test is searchable, its measurements side by side with the model's verdict.
The suppressant lab compares carbon dioxide and helium, and honestly admits when the data cannot rank them.
Similar Tests finds the closest real experiments to any condition you can imagine.
Ask FlameGuard searches NASA's report for you, and points to the exact page.
The science is explained too, with every claim linked to its source.
It even flags its own weak spots. NASA reported contaminated fuel needles, so every methanol prediction shows how much that could change the answer.
What does this change? Fire safety evidence from orbit becomes something mission designers, teachers and students can explore in seconds, uncertainty included.
Next, FlameGuard needs more data: cleaner tests, more fuels, burning solid materials, and review by combustion scientists.
One day, a tool like this could check every proposed spacecraft atmosphere against real evidence, before a crew ever breathes it.
FlameGuard A I. Fire safety intelligence for space exploration. I'm Fahim Foysal. Thank you.
